tools.name: adapt_example_trajectory
tools.title: Adapt an example's trajectory
tools.summary: For the same task with the same objects in a new initial layout: re-anchors the example's verified trajectory to where each object now starts (phase by phase, by the example's anchor schedule), re-solves the arms by IK and accepts it only if reach, joint-speed, penetration and object-continuity checks pass.
tools.description: The example's trajectory proved a set of hand-object relative motions; they stay valid when an object starts a few centimetres or degrees elsewhere, as long as each hand follows the object it works on. The layout is per movable object (dx, dy, dyaw_deg) relative to the example's frame-0 placement: give it, or give the run's Stage 2 scene_recon.json and it is computed from the objects' poses (matched by Stage 1 id). This is the Stage 4 randomization machinery applied to one chosen layout, so it takes seconds, not a solve. On success it writes trajectory.npz, the adapted scene (objects fixed to the world moved) and adapt_report.json; on failure the report names the failed checks (reach, speed, penetration, continuity) and the frames, and the subgoals are solved normally.

inputs.name: example
inputs.description: Example folder (from find_example).

inputs.name: workspace
inputs.description: Where to write the adapted trajectory.

inputs.name: layout
inputs.description: {body: [dx, dy, dyaw_deg]} for the example's movable objects.

inputs.name: scene_recon_json
inputs.description: The run's Stage 2 manifest, to compute the layout from.

inputs.name: checks
inputs.description: Override the check tolerances (ik_pos_tol_m, ik_rot_tol_deg, penetration_tol_m, ...).

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: ok, failed checks, layout, report, trajectory path, adapted scene path.

tools.name: adapt_trajectory_to_layout
tools.title: Adapt trajectory to layout
tools.summary: Re-anchor a verified episode to displaced objects (object-anchored trajectory warping), re-solve the arms by IK and accept only layouts that pass the feasibility checks.
tools.description: Loads the scene and the verified qpos trajectory, discovers each end effector's chain and the arm bolted to it (a position-only weld or connect leaves the arm's orientation free), and builds a per-frame anchor schedule per side from segments given by phase-label patterns or frame ranges: anchor = one object or 'world', or a smoothstep blend from one anchor to another. Anchors may only change through a blend, otherwise the hand would jump; the schedule is validated. For a layout (dx, dy, dyaw per object, a joint-space start offset per arm that fades out before the first contact phase) it displaces every anchored end-effector frame rigidly, re-solves the end effector and the arm by IK with retries, moves a carried object with its carrier from the frame it first moves until its release phase (then it rests with whatever its carrier was anchored to), moves static objects in the model, and runs the checks: IK reach (2 mm, 1 deg), joint speed (1.5 x original + 0.5), object step continuity (10 mm), and penetration on all visible geometry relative to the original (3 mm). adapt_trajectory_to_layout draws layouts from ranges until num_samples pass and writes each as trajectory.npz + sample.json. A zero layout reproduces the input exactly.

inputs.name: scene
inputs.description: MJCF scene (.xml; the penetration check recompiles it).

inputs.name: trajectory
inputs.description: trajectory.npz with qpos, labels, fps.

inputs.name: end_effectors
inputs.description: Hand root per side.

inputs.name: objects
inputs.description: Objects that may be displaced; carrier = side that moves it; release = phase pattern or frame where it is put down; attached_to = rides another object's start.

inputs.name: segments
inputs.type: dict side -> list[{phases | frames, anchor | blend}]
inputs.description: Anchor schedule per side.

inputs.name: ranges
inputs.description: Sampling ranges (metres, degrees) for adapt_trajectory_to_layout.

inputs.name: num_samples, max_attempts, seed, init_jitter_rad, init_blend_frames
inputs.description: Sampling controls. Defaults 1, 50, 0, 0.05, 45.

inputs.name: checks
inputs.description: Override ik_pos_tol_m, ik_rot_tol_deg, joint_speed_scale, joint_speed_floor, penetration_tol_m, object_step_tol_m.

inputs.name: out_dir
inputs.description: Where samples are written.

inputs.name: include_original
inputs.description: Default False.

outputs.name: samples
outputs.description: Per accepted sample: layout, qpos [T, nq], body_overrides for static objects, checks report, path.

outputs.name: summary
outputs.description: accepted, attempts, rejected reasons per attempt.

tools.name: add_connector_latch
tools.title: Add a connector latch (plug held in its port)
tools.summary: Writes the spring latch of a plug-in connector (a USB-C plug in a phone) into a staged Stage 2 scene: an inactive weld between the port body and the plug body that the Stage 3 executor switches on when the plug bottoms out in the port and off when it is pulled out harder than release_N; returns the executor rule and the scene_recon.json fields that carry it.
tools.description: A real USB-C plug is held by spring latches, not by friction alone, and a gram-scale friction fit is fragile in contact physics (its hold depends on the contact softness, the noslip iterations and the timestep). The latch is the executor's run-time rule kind 'latch' (common.episode.latch_rules_live / latch_step, applied every physics step by servo_rollout in Stage 3 and in Stage 4's physics replay): when the plug tip site is within seat_m of the port floor site, axes within 20 degrees, has stopped advancing and no longer presses on the port harder than 1 N (so the push of the hand that seated it is not locked in: a plug the hand still presses latches when the hand lets go), the weld's relpose is set to the bodies' current relative pose and the weld is switched on (no snap); when the weld carries a pull-out load (its force on the plug along the port's insertion axis, low-passed over 5 ms) above release_N it is switched off and stays off until the plug has left the port. An engaged latch is handed from subgoal to subgoal. This skill writes the weld into the scene file (body1 = port body, body2 = plug body, anchor at the plug tip site, relpose = the seated pose: the tip site's frame on the floor site's frame turned roll_deg about the insertion axis, torquescale 1, a nearly hard solref / solimp, active=false; a scene whose video starts with the plug in its port gives active=True and the relpose is read from keyframe `key`, where the plug must be seated). It re-compiles the scene and checks the weld. Copy `scene_fields` into the plug's (the cable's) scene_recon.json entry: execute_subgoal_plan (latch_rules_from_recon) and write_stage4_config read the rule from the entry's `latch`. construct_phone's <name>_port_floor and construct_plug_cable's <name>_plug_tip are the two sites (with the scene's name prefix after stage_on_bench); prove the port with plug_port_retention_test, whose default trials run the same latch rule in the episode's physics.

inputs.name: scene
inputs.description: Staged Stage 2 scene MJCF (scene.xml after stage_on_bench).

inputs.name: plug_body
inputs.description: Body that carries the plug (construct_plug_cable's plug.body, scene-prefixed).

inputs.name: plug_site
inputs.description: Site at the plug tip, z along the insertion direction, on plug_body (construct_plug_cable's plug.tip_site).

inputs.name: port_body
inputs.description: Body that carries the port (construct_phone's body, scene-prefixed).

inputs.name: port_site
inputs.description: Site on the port floor, z along the insertion direction, on port_body (construct_phone's sites.port_floor).

inputs.name: out_xml
inputs.description: Where to write the scene with the latch. Default: scene itself (in place).

inputs.name: name
inputs.description: Weld name. Default latch_<plug_body>. A weld of that name already in the scene is replaced.

inputs.name: seat_m
inputs.description: Tip-to-floor distance that counts as seated, m. Default 0.0015

inputs.name: release_N
inputs.description: Pull-out load at which the latch lets go, N (USB-C: 8-20 N). Default 15

inputs.name: roll_deg
inputs.description: Roll of the seated plug about the insertion axis relative to the floor site's frame (a reversible plug seats at 0 or 180). Default 0

inputs.name: active
inputs.description: Start the latch engaged (the plug sits in its port at keyframe `key`). Default false

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: Keyframe read when active=True. Default 0

inputs.name: solref, solimp
inputs.description: Weld softness. Default [0.004, 1] and [0.998, 0.999, 0.001, 0.5, 2] (about 0.006 mm per N on a 6 g plug).

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: xml (the written scene), equality, rule ({kind: 'latch', eq, site_a, site_b, seat_m, release_N}: the executor rule), scene_fields ({latch: {eq, site_a, site_b, seat_m, release_N, plug_body, port_body}}: copy into the plug's scene_recon.json entry), eq_data (anchor 3, relpose 7, torquescale 1), check {active0, quat_norm, torquescale, seated_gap_m (active=True)}.

tools.cli: python -m tool_library.skills.add_connector_latch scene.xml plug_body plug_site port_body port_site

tools.name: add_wrist_cameras
tools.title: Add wrist cameras
tools.summary: Derives a wrist-camera pose for each hand from its own fingertip sites (overhand palm view or behind-the-palm view) and adds the cameras plus optional fixed cameras, leaving nq and every body pose unchanged.
tools.description: Hard-coded camera offsets do not transfer between hands: on one dexterous hand the two sides' local frames differed by a 90 deg rotation, not a mirror. So the frame is read from the fingertips: the mean finger direction is the hand axis, the index-to-pinky row is the image horizontal, and up points away from the thumb (back of hand). 'overhand' puts the lens on the palm looking out along the fingers, as on the real rig footage; 'behind' puts it behind the palm looking into the grasp volume. Cameras and the optional mount geometry are jointless and non-colliding, so a qpos recorded before the cameras existed replays frame for frame.

inputs.name: scene
inputs.description: Scene MJCF.

inputs.name: out_xml
inputs.description: Output MJCF with the cameras.

inputs.name: hands
inputs.description: {side: {'body': hand root body, 'fingertips': {'thumb','index','middle','ring','pinky': site names}}}.

inputs.name: mode
inputs.description: 'overhand' (default) or 'behind'.

inputs.name: fovy
inputs.description: Vertical field of view in degrees (100 overhand, 70 behind).

inputs.name: fixed
inputs.description: {name: {'pos', 'target' | 'quat', 'fovy'}} world cameras to add as well.

inputs.name: draw_mount
inputs.description: Add a small visual housing at the camera (default False).

inputs.name: params
inputs.description: Framing: overhand u=0.05 ef=0.055 k=0.45 reach=0.6; behind back=0.155 side=0.048 out=0.012.

outputs.name: info
outputs.description: out_xml, camera names, per-camera local pos/quat, nq unchanged check.

tools.name: analyze_manipulation
tools.title: Analyze manipulation
tools.summary: From per-frame object masks and hand pixel points: contact episodes per hand and object, the manipulating hand by co-motion, and the grasp region on the object.
tools.description: For every frame it builds a distance transform of each object mask and reads the nearest distance of each hand's pixel points to it; a hand touches when that is within contact_px (4) for at least sustain (3) consecutive sampled frames, giving first/last contact frames and the region on the object's bounding box where the first contact happens (as fractions and words such as 'top-left'). Which hand manipulates a moving object is decided by co-motion: over the object's motion window the per-step pixel displacement of the hand centroid and of the object centroid are compared step by step, summing the aligned component; proximity only breaks the tie when no hand moved with the object. Object world positions, when given, provide the motion window (6 cm, 4 frames), travel, start/end and lift. Inputs are arrays and dictionaries, so any detector, hand estimator and camera work.

inputs.name: object_masks
inputs.type: dict name -> ndarray [T, H, W] bool | callable(name, t)
inputs.description: Per-frame object masks.

inputs.name: hand_points
inputs.description: Pixel points of each hand per frame (projected mesh vertices, keypoints).

inputs.name: object_positions
inputs.description: World positions per frame (camera-motion compensated), for motion window and travel.

inputs.name: contact_px, sustain, stride
inputs.description: Contact distance, persistence, frame stride. Defaults 4, 3, auto (~110 samples).

inputs.name: n_frames
inputs.description: Default None.

outputs.name: report
outputs.description: objects: moved, motion_window, start/end, travel, lift, manipulated_by, hand_evidence; hands: touches per object with first/last contact frame, contact frames, grasp_region_on_object; look_at_frames.

tools.name: anchor_cord_end_to_body
tools.title: Anchor a cord end to a fixed object
tools.summary: Welds one end link of a cord (rope, thread, cable) to the body of a FIXED scene object (a tape dispenser, a clamp, a post) with an active weld whose relative pose is taken from keyframe 0, refusing the world, the table, the robot and mocap bodies.
tools.description: Loads the scene, resets it to keyframe `key` (or qpos0 when it has none), and reads the pose of cord_body relative to anchor_body. It refuses an anchor that is the world body, a mocap body, a body that can move (any joint in its chain to the world), a robot body (name starting with robot_prefix) or a table/floor (name containing one of forbidden_words): only a fixed object's own body can hold a cord end. The cord body must be able to move. It then adds <weld body1=anchor_body body2=cord_body relpose=...> (relpose = the cord link's pose in the anchor body's frame at the keyframe, so it is never taken from qpos0; the weld point is body2's origin, i.e. the cord end itself, so the light link cannot swing about the fixed object's distant origin) to the MJCF's <equality> section, stiff by default (solref [2 timestep, 1], solimp 0.99/0.999 over 0.1 mm, so a light end link gives only a fraction of a millimetre under a hand's pull), writes out_xml and re-compiles it: the equality's residual at the keyframe must be below 1e-6 m (and 1e-4 rad for a weld), otherwise it raises. Keyframes are untouched (an equality adds no state). Anchor the cable's ROOT link (the body carrying its free joint) when possible: a weld on a link deep in a nested MuJoCo cable acts through every joint above it and gives millimetres under a pull where one on the root gives microns; the result lists that as a warning. Assumes the scene is one MJCF file (as stage_on_bench writes it).

inputs.name: scene_xml
inputs.description: The scene MJCF holding both bodies.

inputs.name: out_xml
inputs.description: Where to write the anchored scene (may be scene_xml itself).

inputs.name: cord_body
inputs.description: The cord's end link body to anchor.

inputs.name: anchor_body
inputs.description: The fixed object's body that holds it.

inputs.name: name
inputs.description: Equality name; default '<cord_body>_anchor'.

inputs.name: key
inputs.description: Keyframe whose state defines the relative pose. Default 0

inputs.name: solref
inputs.description: Equality solref; None gives [2 x timestep, 1]. Default None

inputs.name: solimp
inputs.description: Equality solimp. Default [0.99, 0.999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2]

inputs.name: robot_prefix
inputs.description: Body-name prefix of the robot (refused as an anchor). Default robot_

inputs.name: forbidden_words
inputs.description: Anchor names containing any of these are refused (the table, the floor). Default ['table', 'floor', 'ground']

outputs.name: anchored
outputs.description: out_xml, equality (name), kind ('weld'), cord_body, anchor_body, relpose [x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz] (the cord link's pose in the anchor body's frame), residual_m, residual_rad, key, warnings (e.g. the anchored link is not the cable's root).

tools.name: attach_arms
tools.title: Attach arms
tools.summary: Search the base pose (x, y, yaw) of an arm so its tip tracks a hand's recorded path, fit all frames, and write the mounted scene with the tip welded to the hand.
tools.description: Reads the hand body's world pose track from the trajectory (or takes an explicit pose path), estimates the arm's reach from its kinematics, and scores candidate bases on rings around the path's centroid (radius fractions of the reach, n_yaw headings each facing the centroid plus facing_offset_deg for assets whose zero yaw does not point along the first link). Each candidate is scored by the arm's IK residual on subsampled frames (position in mm plus 3 x tilt degrees), a penalty for joints within 5 degrees of a stop, and a penalty for the tip falling below the table. The best few are refined with Nelder-Mead, the winner is fitted on every frame (trust-region warm starts, branch resets blended), and the scene is rewritten with the root body moved and a weld (torquescale 0 when position_only) between the tip and the hand. An optional hand offset gives the flange pose in the hand frame.

inputs.name: scene
inputs.description: MJCF scene containing the arm and the hand.

inputs.name: trajectory
inputs.description: qpos trajectory the hand path is read from.

inputs.name: arm_root, arm_tip, hand_body
inputs.description: World-fixed root body of the arm, its flange body, the hand body it should carry.

inputs.name: hand_offset
inputs.description: Flange pose in the hand frame; default identity.

inputs.name: poses
inputs.description: Explicit flange path instead of the trajectory.

inputs.name: base_z, candidates, facing_offset_deg, position_only
inputs.description: Mount height (default the root's), ring search, yaw convention, weld type.

inputs.name: table_top_z
inputs.description: Penalize tips below this.

inputs.name: out_scene
inputs.description: Write the mounted scene here.

inputs.name: n_score_frames
inputs.description: Default 24.

inputs.name: refine_top
inputs.description: Default 3.

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: base_pos, base_yaw_deg, residual {pos_mm max/p95, tilt_deg max}, resets, qpos [T, n] arm joints, joint_names, candidates tried, out_scene.

tools.name: bench_tool_large_arena
tools.title: Bench tool with a large arena
tools.summary: Run any library skill or verifier that loads a bench scene from its MJCF (the subgoal executor, the planner's preview, the episode audits) with every model compiled during the call given a larger MuJoCo arena, so contact-dense states (a lid seated on a rim, snap latches pressed over their nubs, many small geoms touching at once) do not abort the call with mj_stackAlloc overflow.
tools.description: MuJoCo sizes the arena (the memory for contacts and constraints) from the model unless the MJCF sets <size memory>. A bench scene whose state packs hundreds of contacts (a lid with a gasket seated on a rim, a strap pressed over a nub, a hand on top of both) can overflow it inside mj_forward, and the FatalError kills the whole tool call even though nothing is wrong with the plan or the physics (the same frames run cleanly with more memory). For the duration of one call of the named tool this wrapper makes every model compiled through mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path, mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string and mujoco.MjSpec.compile get at least `memory_mb` megabytes of arena (a model that already asks for more keeps its own), then restores the original loaders, also when the tool raises. The tool's own arguments pass through unchanged and its result is returned verbatim, with the arena size used and how many models were compiled during the call. Nothing about the physics changes: only the memory available for contacts and constraints. It does not edit any scene file.

inputs.name: tool
inputs.description: Name of a library skill or verifier (e.g. execute_subgoal_plan, preview_keyframes, episode_physics_check).

inputs.name: args
inputs.description: The tool's own arguments, passed through unchanged.

inputs.name: memory_mb
inputs.description: Minimum arena per compiled model in megabytes. Default 256.

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: {result: the tool's return value verbatim, tool, memory_mb, models_compiled}.

tools.name: build_cord_planning_scene
tools.title: Build cord planning scene
tools.summary: Writes a copy of the Stage 2 scene with every cord that Isaac Sim simulates added as a MuJoCo planning copy (construct_rope-named links at the cord's settled, or a recorded, state), so execute_subgoal_plan's rope moves (lay, drag, pin) can pinch and carry its links; the cord's physics of record stays Isaac Sim's.
tools.description: Deformables are simulated in Isaac Sim (Stage 2's cord_json; execute_isaac_deformables in Stage 3). The executor's rope moves and plan_knot_moves address a cable's links by body name, so this tool adds each Isaac cord to a copy of scene.xml as a chain of the same links (construct_rope's names <name>B_first .. B_last, ball joints with light damping), laid at the cord's settled Stage 2 state, or at `state` (a recording's frame: after an earlier move, plan the next one from where Isaac Sim left the cord: state={'recording': isaac/isaac_recording.npz, 'frame': -1}). Execute the robot in this scene, then run execute_isaac_deformables on the executed scene and trajectory: the planning copy's columns are overwritten by the Isaac recording in the mirror the gates read, so what MuJoCo did to the copy is never evidence. Returns the scene path and the cords' body names.

inputs.name: scene_recon_json
inputs.description: Stage 2 scene_recon.json (its Isaac deformables and scene.xml).

inputs.name: out_xml
inputs.description: The scene to write (keyframes extended with the cords' state).

inputs.name: scene_xml
inputs.description: The scene to extend; default the Stage 2 scene.xml.

inputs.name: state
inputs.description: {recording, frame}: lay the cords as an Isaac recording left them. Default the settled Stage 2 state.

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: scene (path), cords {name: [link body names]}, slices {name: [first, last + 1] qpos}.

tools.name: build_isaac_scene
tools.title: Build Isaac Sim scene
tools.summary: Exports a MuJoCo scene (robot, table, rigid objects at a given state) to Isaac Sim 5.0, adds each deformable cord (rope, cable, string) as a chain of capsule rigid bodies on D6 joints with bending stiffness and joint friction laid along its measured centreline, settles under PhysX gravity, renders through the registered camera, and saves the USD stage, the settled centrelines and a drift report.
tools.description: The deformable route of Stage 2: non-deformable objects are reconstructed and placed in MuJoCo; a scene with a rope-like object is then rebuilt in Isaac Sim with the same bench, camera and placement so the cord can be simulated with PhysX. The export reads every visible geom of the scene at `qpos` (boxes, capsules, cylinders, spheres, meshes with their vertices), the table gets collision, rigid objects get convex-hull collision, robot geoms are visual. Each deformable is {name, points (N, 3) in the rig frame, radius, rgb, density, fix_start, fix_end, bend_stiffness, bend_damping, joint_friction} plus, optionally, `preset` ('thin_cord', the default: 8 mm heavily damped links for cords of a few millimetres; 'segmented_rope': the coefficient set fitted on a real 27.7 mm velvet rope, 27 mm links, self-colliding, sticky table and slippery rope-on-rope contact), `physics` (overrides of any coefficient of tool_library.common.isaac_cord.PRESETS), `n_links`, `cap_rgb` with `cap_length_a_m` / `cap_length_b_m` (rigid end caps: their colour) and `grasp` (how Stage 3's hands hold it); every cord is built by isaac_cord.build_cord, the builder Stage 3's Isaac episodes and Stage 4's replays use. `junction` {center, radius, rgb} ties several strands to one small body (a knot). An explicit n_links wins and a preset other than thin_cord takes its own link length; for thin cords the LINK LENGTH RULE: links are 8 mm long unless that makes more than `max_links` (default 80) links in one articulation (a cord, or all strands tied to one junction); then the cord is split into exactly max_links equal links (a 1.9 m cord gets 24 mm links). Measured on a 1.25 mm cord: 110 links settle, 120 explode (drift 1e7 m), 128-206 make PhysX report invalid transforms and leave the cord where it was laid, 300 crash Isaac; a 6 mm cord holds 206 but not 300. An explicit `segment_m` that needs more than max_links links is refused. 1/480 s TGS, settled for `settle_s`. A run is refused (RuntimeError naming the issue) when PhysX logs invalid transforms or errors, a settled centreline is non-finite, a chain is torn (neighbouring links further apart than one link length) or the cord moved more than `max_mean_drift_m` on average while settling; the report is still written with ok false and the issues. COLOUR: a cord's rgb goes to a UsdPreviewSurface diffuseColor (0..255 values are scaled to 0..1) and renders as that colour; a cord thinner than about 3 mm is a couple of pixels wide, and its hard shadow from the key light, as wide as the cord, made it read as nearly black, so thin cords cast no shadow by default (cord_cast_shadows). Runs the Isaac script in the Isaac Sim Python given by `isaac_python`, DEXAGENT_ISAAC_PYTHON or dexagent.yaml, with HOME redirected to `isaac_home` (Isaac writes gigabytes of cache) and the EULA accepted. Returns the render, the stage path, per-cord link counts and the mean drift during settling (a cord laid on the table should drift millimetres; centimetres mean it was floating or interpenetrating), and per cord `<tag>_<name>_cord.json`: the resolved specification with the SETTLED link poses (centres and orientations), which a Stage 2 entry with simulator 'isaac' names as isaac.cord_json and from which Stage 3 (execute_isaac_deformables) starts.

inputs.name: scene_xml
inputs.description: The MuJoCo scene (bench + rigid objects).

inputs.name: camera
inputs.description: camera.json in the rig frame.

inputs.name: deformables
inputs.description: Cords to add: name, points [[x,y,z],...] rig metres, radius, rgb, density (1100), fix_start, fix_end, bend_stiffness (0.004), bend_damping (0.002), joint_friction (0.0015); optional preset ('thin_cord' | 'segmented_rope'), physics overrides, n_links, cap_rgb, cap_length_a_m, cap_length_b_m, grasp.

inputs.name: out_dir
inputs.description: Receives export.json, <tag>_sim.png, <tag>_scene.usda, <tag>_report.json, settled centrelines.

inputs.name: qpos
inputs.description: Scene state to export (npy or list); default the model's initial state.

inputs.name: junction
inputs.description: {center, radius, rgb}: a small rigid body the strands' first links are jointed to.

inputs.name: segment_m
inputs.description: Link length in metres. Default None = the link length rule: 8 mm, lengthened so no articulation has more than max_links links.

inputs.name: max_links
inputs.description: Most links PhysX gets in one articulation (one cord, or every strand tied to one junction). Default 80.

inputs.name: max_mean_drift_m
inputs.description: A cord whose links move more than this on average while settling (it was floating, buried or blew up) fails the run. Default 0.10.

inputs.name: cord_cast_shadows
inputs.description: Whether cord links cast shadows. Default None: only cords of radius >= 3 mm do (a thinner cord is a few pixels wide and its hard shadow strip beside it makes it read as black).

inputs.name: settle_s
inputs.description: Settling time under gravity. Default 1.5.

inputs.name: self_collision
inputs.description: Cord self-collision between its own links, for every cord. Default None: each cord's preset decides (thin_cord off: its 8 mm links overlap and would push the chain apart; segmented_rope on: its capsules are trimmed so non-neighbours never touch at rest). The table and the rigid objects always collide with every link.

inputs.name: tag
inputs.description: Output file prefix. Default 'isaac'.

inputs.name: isaac_python
inputs.description: Isaac Sim's Python; default DEXAGENT_ISAAC_PYTHON.

inputs.name: isaac_home
inputs.description: HOME for Isaac's caches; default DEXAGENT_ISAAC_HOME or out_dir/isaac_home.

inputs.name: timeout_s
inputs.description: Default 1800.

inputs.name: frame
inputs.description: Video frame for a 50/50 overlay of the render.

inputs.name: exclude_bodies
inputs.description: Body name prefixes left out of the export (bodies named like a deformable are always left out: Isaac rebuilds the cord).

outputs.name: sim_png / scene_usda / report_json / export_json
outputs.description: Written files.

outputs.name: cord_json
outputs.description: {cord name: <tag>_<name>_cord.json}: the resolved specification (schema dexagent.isaac_cord.v1) with link_poses {centres, quats} of the settled state.

outputs.name: report
outputs.description: ok, issues; per cord: n_links, segment_m, length_m, radius_m, preset, finite, mean_drift_m, max_drift_m, link_stretch, min_z_m, settled_centreline, settled_quats; '_' holds settle_s, physics_dt, physx_invalid_transforms, physx_errors.

tools.name: build_isaac_scene_soft_bodies
tools.title: Build Isaac scene with compact soft bodies
tools.summary: Exports a MuJoCo scene to Isaac Sim with each compact soft object (plush, sponge) as a dynamic PhysX body of its own geoms on a compliant-contact material, settles it, renders through the video camera and reports each soft body's settling drift.
tools.description: The cord route (build_isaac_scene) only rebuilds rope-like deformables; compact soft objects such as stuffed toys are modelled in MuJoCo as light free bodies with soft contact (solref time constant and damping ratio). This tool carries the same model into PhysX. Every visible geom of the scene at its initial keyframe (or `qpos`) is exported in the rig frame, as build_isaac_scene does (table with collision and friction, other non-robot objects with static convex-hull collision). Each body named in `soft_bodies` is left out of the static export and rebuilt as ONE dynamic rigid body at its MuJoCo pose and mass: boxes, spheres, capsules and cylinders as USD primitives, ellipsoids and meshes as convex-hull meshes, visual-only geoms without collision. Its physics material is compliant: stiffness k = m (2 pi / tc)^2 and damping c = 2 zeta m (2 pi / tc), with tc and zeta read from the geoms' solref (or given per body), so a palm pressing it sinks as in MuJoCo. The scene settles for `settle_s` under gravity; the report gives per soft body the start and end position, mean_drift_m (= max_drift_m, one body), the rotation change and the contact parameters. The Isaac script is written next to the export and run with Isaac Sim's Python. Assumes rig frame = stage frame, z up, metres.

tools.name: construct_articulated
tools.title: Construct articulated cabinet
tools.summary: Measured dims + a top-to-bottom drawer grid + measured colours -> ArtiCraft model.py compiled through ArtiCraft's geometry QC to a URDF with prismatic drawers and finger-clearing pulls; a built-in URDF writer when ArtiCraft is absent.
tools.description: Writes a parametric model.py against the ArtiCraft SDK: a carcass of five panels with shelf webs between rows and dividers between columns, one drawer box per cell (front, two sides, back, bottom) with two posts and a pull bar standing max(32 mm, 6 x bar radius) proud of the front, and a PRISMATIC articulation per drawer along +y with limits 0..travel_frac x depth. Panel thickness, row gap, side clearance and reveal scale with the dims. With backend='articraft' (default when ARTICRAFT_DIR or `articraft_dir` points at a checkout) the model is copied into a fresh record, compiled with `cli.compile_record`, and accepted only on 'failures=0': ArtiCraft's checks that no parts overlap in sampled poses, that joint origins lie on geometry and that each drawer moves >= 0.5 x travel along +y. With backend='builtin' the identical geometry is emitted as a URDF by this file (same names, materials and joints), so the tool works without ArtiCraft. Either way the result lists the joint names ('carcass_to_drawer_r<i>c<j>'), the moving joint, the measured layout actually built, and closed/open preview PNGs rendered with MuJoCo. Colours are not defaulted silently: body_rgba and front_rgba should come from a colour measurement of the video, and the handle must differ from the body (a pull is too small to appear in a palette, so it is read by eye: black ~[0.05,0.05,0.05,1], steel ~[0.75,0.75,0.78,1]).

tools.name: construct_bead_pile
tools.title: Construct a bead pile
tools.summary: A heap of many small beads (or similar small parts) as one body: visual bead cylinders laid in a measured elliptical footprint with a measured colour palette, colliding through a few cell boxes, fixed by default, with keep-out spots for separately built free beads.
tools.description: Lays bead centres on a hexagonal grid (spacing 2 * bead_radius * spacing_frac) inside an ellipse of the given length (body x) and width (body y), shrunk by one bead radius so every bead lies inside the footprint, drops the grid points that fall within a keep_out circle (plus one bead radius), and keeps n_beads of them chosen at random with the seed (all of them when fewer fit; the count built is reported). With layers=2 a second, offset layer of about a third as many beads lies on top of the inner 60 percent of the footprint. Every bead is a visual-only cylinder (contype 0, conaffinity 0, density 0) of bead_radius and bead_height, lying flat, coloured by a seeded draw from the palette (optionally weighted), with an optional dark disk of hole_radius on top that reads as the bead's hole. Collision: with cell > 0 the footprint is divided into square cells of that size and every cell that holds a bead centre becomes one box covering the bounding box of its beads' disks (so the visual beads always lie inside the collision boxes) up to the top of its highest bead; a box that would reach into a keep_out circle is split along its longer side until none does (a lone bead beside the circle collides as its own cylinder), so the free beads in the keep_out spots never start inside the heap's collision; with cell = 0 every bead is its own collision cylinder. The collision geoms carry the whole mass, which is the beads' plastic volume (outer cylinder minus hole) times bead_density, so the heap weighs what its beads do. The body is fixed to the world by default (a heap is not carried; a fixed heap does not slide off as one lump when a finger brushes it); fixed=False gives it a free joint. The body origin is the footprint centre on the table (z = 0 at the bead bottoms). Assumes beads lie flat in one or two layers; the loose-bead dynamics of a real heap (spreading when stirred) are not modelled.

tools.summary: A parametric bottle whose cap is held on by a real thread: rotation and lift are coupled, and the cap cannot come off without turning.
tools.description: Builds the bottle as a lathe mesh over primitive colliders and the cap as a free body with a hollow skirt, from one dictionary of numbers: body radius and height, shoulder and neck, cap size and wall, thread pitch and turns, colours, masses, friction. The thread is modelled, because MuJoCo has no screw joint and URDF cannot express one: a carrier body inside the bottle carries a yaw hinge and a lift slide, an equality constraint locks lift = pitch/2pi x yaw, dry friction on the yaw joint makes the thread self-locking (an axial push or pull cannot back-drive it), and a weld between carrier and cap is the engagement, which disengages when the cap has travelled thread_pitch x thread_turns. A visible helical ridge is drawn on the neck. The asset has no actuators; the only way to open it is torque on the cap. Every parameter is written to <name>_params.json so a build can be repeated or refitted by editing numbers. The thread_self_locking_test verifier proves a built bottle.

tools.name: construct_conical_tube_rack
tools.title: Construct rack for 15 ml conical tubes
tools.summary: An open-frame rack for 15 ml conical tubes: top plate with round holes, catch plate, posts and perforated walls, every touchable part a box collider.
tools.description: Builds the moulded open frame as box colliders (plates, posts, walls) with visual-only perforations and hole rims, from its footprint, height, hole grid and colours. Holes are indexed by row and column; hole_xy() and hole_top_z() return where a tube stands so a trajectory can address a well by index. The bottom plate is flat: something standing leaning in a well (a pipette, a cone tip) is held sideways by friction only and creeps out within seconds under MuJoCo's soft friction; when an object must stand in a well like that, or a robot hand works near the rack (its top plate is four boxes per well), use construct_conical_tube_rack_lowpoly (merged top plate, catch holes in the bottom plate under chosen wells) instead.

tools.name: construct_cup
tools.title: Construct cup
tools.summary: Parametric cup/tumbler/mug from base radius, rim radius, height (or a wall profile) with a hollow collision model: base disk plus convex wall wedges.
tools.description: Builds a solid of revolution from a (radius, height) wall profile, a straight frustum between base_radius and rim_radius by default. The visual is a watertight shell with a rolled lip and a separate interior lining mesh (so the inside has its own colour); the collision is a base disk plus n_wedges convex hulls of the wall between adjacent rays, which keeps the mouth open and the interior empty for stacking, filling and placing in bowls. Mass follows from density over the wedges or is set directly. An optional handle (ring of capsules tangent to the wall) turns it into a mug. The body gets a freejoint unless fixed. Sites mark the rim centre and the inner floor. The same builder underlies construct_bowl with a curved profile.

tools.name: construct_cup_upside_down
tools.title: Upside-down cup (mouth on the table)
tools.summary: A construct_cup vessel turned mouth-down: the open rim rests on the support and the closed base faces up, with the body origin at the rim contact so it can be staged at z = 0.
tools.description: Builds the cup with construct_cup from the same parameters (base_radius = the closed base, rim_radius = the open mouth, height, wall, colours, mass, ...) and then wraps every geom and site of the root body in a frame rotated 180 degrees about x and lifted by the height, so the mouth ring sits at body z = 0 and the closed base at z = height. The free joint stays on the root body, so the asset is staged with stage_on_bench like any standing object and needs no roll. Collision stays the hollow wedge model (the inside under the cup is empty). A params json with upside_down = true is written next to the XML. Assumes MuJoCo >= 3.1 (<frame> element). Unknown parameters raise ValueError (they are passed to construct_cup's validation).

inputs.description: Directory for the XML, meshes and params json.

inputs.name: params
inputs.description: Any construct_cup parameter (name, base_radius = closed base radius, rim_radius = mouth radius, height, wall, lip, bottom, body_rgba, inner_rgba, mass, density, friction, condim, pos, yaw_deg, fixed, include_floor, ...).

tools.name: construct_cuttable_rope
tools.title: Construct cuttable rope
tools.summary: A rope that can be cut in MuJoCo: two elastic cables built along the measured centreline, split at the cut location and tied there by one CONNECT equality, as one MJCF that stage_on_bench stages like construct_rope; returns the Stage 2 manifest fields (cut_joins, halves) Stage 3 needs to cut it.
tools.description: MuJoCo cannot break a body chain at run time, so a rope the task cuts is authored as two cables and one CONNECT equality at the cut point; switching the equality off is the cut, and the Stage 3 executor (execute_subgoal_plan) does it through scissors.try_sever only when the blades have closed on the join (in their span, wedge and plane, closing, biting). The measured centreline (measure_rope output, a hand trace back-projected to the table, any polyline in rig metres) is densified, crossings of the rope with itself are lifted (the later strand over the earlier one by one diameter), and the polyline is split at the cut location: an arc-length fraction (cut_frac) or the rope point nearest a world point (cut_point). Each half is BUILT along its own piece (cable vertices), so qpos0 is the measured shape, both halves end exactly on the cut point (continuous at the join in the reference pose the CONNECT is baked from) and every keyframe stage_on_bench writes already has the rope laid where the video has it, with no keyframe editing. The two capsules at the join do not collide with each other (an exclude); everything else self-collides as in construct_rope. Stage it with stage_on_bench at x = y = z = 0, yaw 0 under the name `scene_name`; `scene_fields` in the result holds root_body, bodies, halves {a, b: root_body, first, last, bodies} and cut_joins [{eq, body, anchor_local, diameter_m, s_m, point, other_body}] in the staged scene names: copy them into the object's scene_recon.json entry (Stage 3 reads `cut_joins`). For an Isaac render of the same rope, build_isaac_scene takes the staged scene as usual.

inputs.description: Cut at the rope point nearest this world point instead (wins over cut_frac).

tools.name: construct_hinged_lid_box
tools.title: Hinged-lid box with a set initial lid state
tools.summary: A rigid box (base tray with four walls) whose lid is hinged along the top of the back wall, optionally with a creased skirt on the lid's free edge, built so that the asset's initial state (qpos0) already shows the lid at a measured opening angle.
tools.description: A gift box, shoebox or chest: the base and its four walls are one rigid body, the lid is a child body on ONE revolute joint along the top outer edge of the back (+y) wall, and an optional skirt is a second revolute crease on the lid's free edge that folds down over the outside of the front wall. Joint angles: lid 0 = shut on the walls, 90 = vertical, 180 = folded flat behind the box at hinge height; skirt 0 = in plane with the lid, 90 = square to it (down the front face when shut, straight up when the lid is folded back). Unlike a box built shut, the lid and skirt bodies are written AT their initial angles and each joint's `ref` equals that angle, so a scene that starts from qpos0 (or a keyframe padded with qpos0) shows the open lid of the first video frame while joint value 0 still means shut. lid_init_deg='rest' computes the angle past 180 at which the lid's free edge rests on the plane under the base (a lid folded back onto the table). Shut is a hard joint stop (stiff solreflimit); lid-vs-base and skirt-vs-base contacts are excluded because hinge and crease are one piece of board. Assumes a rectangular box, uniform board thickness.

tools.name: construct_magnetic_ring
tools.title: Construct a magnetic ring
tools.summary: A hollow rigid ring (short tube) as a free body whose outer surface magnetically clings rim to rim to other rings built by this skill, so rings can hang from, roll around and be pulled off one another.
tools.description: Builds one MJCF holding a single ring: n_segments box geoms arranged around the axis between inner_radius and outer_radius over the ring's height (hollow bore, the mass split evenly over the wall), on a free body whose origin is the point that rests on the table (bottom centre when the axis is vertical, the lowest rim point when the ring stands on its rim with the axis horizontal). Every accent_every-th segment takes accent_rgba so the pattern reads in renders. The magnet is a jointless child body '<name>_magnet' carrying a sphere (default; or a cylinder over the wall height) of radius outer_radius + magnet_pad_m in its own collision bit (magnet_bit): magnet shells collide only with each other, with margin = gap = magnet_range_m so a contact appears just before touching without pushing. A <general> actuator with body transmission on that child, gainprm 0 and biasprm [magnet_force_N] applies MuJoCo adhesion with a constant force: the ring is pulled toward every magnet shell it touches, the force split over its magnet contacts. Two touching rings therefore attract with about twice magnet_force_N, a ring hangs from another, rolls around its rim, and separates under a larger pull. A sphere magnet keeps the centres at a fixed distance whatever the tilt, so a ring wedged between two others cannot be levered out of plane by edge contacts (a cylinder magnet can). Assumes all rings of a scene are built by this skill with the same magnet_bit; the actuator needs no control (ctrl is ignored). magnet_force_N 0 builds the ring without any magnet parts (no child body, shell or actuator).

tools.name: construct_multi_strand_cable
tools.title: Construct multi-strand cable (strands joined at one end, optionally plaited)
tools.summary: Several flexible strands (flat ribbons or round cords) joined at one end by a small knot body, each an elastic MuJoCo cable laid along a measured tail polyline, optionally plaited near the joined end into a three-strand braid with a chosen number of alternating crossings.
tools.description: Builds one free object: a junction body (the knot, stitch or tape that joins the strands) with N elastic cables (mujoco.elasticity.cable) attached to it by ball joints, so the link graph is one connected tree with N free ends. Each strand has its own width, thickness, colour and mass per metre; profile 'flat' makes every link a box (width x thickness, a ribbon or strap that lies flat), 'round' a capsule of radius width/2 (a cord). Strand centrelines come from the caller: either a full 'centreline' per strand starting at the junction, or, with 'braid', a three-strand plait generated along a braid axis polyline (phases 0, 120, 240 degrees: lateral a*sin(t+phi), height b*(1 -/+ sin 2(t+phi))/2, which gives exactly `crossings` alternating crossings, outer strand over the middle for style 'over', under for 'under') followed by each strand's measured 'tail' polyline from the braid's lower end to its tip. Strands are matched to the plait positions by where their tails go (left to right across the axis). Inside the braid the link boxes are narrowed by braid_width_frac (a ribbon bunches in a tight plait) and the lateral amplitude and lift are chosen so that no two strands overlap at rest; crossings between tails on the table are lifted locally, the later strand over the earlier. The asset is written in the frame of the positions given (stage it at x = y = 0, yaw 0 when they are rig coordinates). Self-collision between strands is on (contype/conaffinity 1); adjacent links are excluded by MuJoCo's parent-child rule. MuJoCo's <composite type="cable"> adds a white skin over box links that hides their colour and replaces the geoms in segmentation renders (silhouette checks then see only the end links); this version deletes those skins (keep_skin=False) or paints them the strand colour (keep_skin=True). Assumes the strands rest on a horizontal support at z = 0.

tools.name: construct_plug_cable
tools.title: Construct a cable with a connector plug (USB-C, Lightning, micro-USB, barrel)
tools.summary: A charging or data cable as an elastic MuJoCo cable laid along a measured centreline or a flat non-crossing coil, with a rigid connector plug (tip plus housing) on the end link itself (the rope's link graph stays one jointed chain) whose tip is sized from the mating port minus a clearance, so the plug can be inserted into a built receptacle.
tools.description: Builds the cord with tool_library.common.cable (the construct_rope builder: inextensible capsule chain, bending and twisting stiffness, self-collision, a mocap grip per end) laid at build time along rest vertices, then adds the plug's geoms and sites to the chosen end segment's own body (not a jointless child body, which deformable_topology_check rejects as a rigid part fused to the rope): a box tip of (port_w - 2 clearance) x (port_h - 2 clearance) x tip_len in front of a box housing that is larger than the port so it stops at the receptacle face. The plug frame has +x along the insertion direction (outward from the cord end), +y across the tip's wide side and +z across its thin side; with plug_flat the plug is rolled about the cord axis so its wide side is horizontal (lying flat on the table, as a plug at rest does) and the last vertices are raised so the housing clears the table. Layout: either `centreline` (a polyline in the asset frame, resampled to `segments` evenly spaced vertices) or `coil` (a flat spiral of `turns` turns shrinking inward from an outer ellipse by `pitch_m` per turn, so the loops never cross, plus an optional smooth tail from the outer end to `tail_end`, where the plug end lies). A coiled cord whose loops cross in the video cannot be ordered from one mask; the non-crossing spiral of the same outer extent and loop count is its physically equivalent resting state. Sites: <name>_plug_tip (z axis = insertion direction, x across the tip's thin side, y across its wide side, at the tip's front face: the site_a of the connector latch, add_connector_latch, which holds the plug once it bottoms out in a construct_phone port) and <name>_plug_grip (housing centre). The returned dict keeps construct_rope's keys (xml, params_json, bodies, grips, welds) so cable verifiers and stage_on_bench treat it like a rope; params_json holds the cord-only parameters (rest vertices included) and plug_params_json every parameter.

tools.name: construct_pump_sprayer
tools.title: Construct pump sprayer
tools.summary: A finger-pump spray bottle as a free rigid body whose pump head is a separate body on a preloaded spring slide joint along the bottle axis: pressed down through a short stroke by a finger, it springs back.
tools.description: Builds one MJCF: a cylindrical bottle body (with a visual colour band), a shoulder, neck and collar, and a pump head (stem, actuator cylinder and a side nozzle) as a child body on a slide joint along the bottle's z axis. The joint range is [-stroke, 0]; its spring has stiffness `spring_stiffness` and a springref placed above the top stop so the head rests at 0 with `preload_N` pressing it against the stop: a finger must exceed the preload to start the stroke and needs preload + stiffness * stroke to bottom out; released, it returns. Geom densities are set so the body and head weigh `mass` and `head_mass`; the body-head contact pair is excluded explicitly (the parent filter does not apply once the bottle is welded to the world). The bottle origin is the centre of its base, z up; the nozzle points along +x rotated by `nozzle_azimuth_deg`. Sites: press (top of the head), nozzle (tip), grasp (mid body). Assumes a round bottle; sizes in metres. Unknown parameters and inconsistent sizes raise ValueError.

tools.name: construct_rope
tools.title: Construct rope or cable
tools.summary: A deformable rope, cord or cable: an elastic MuJoCo cable of N capsule segments, inextensible, bending with measured stiffness and colliding with itself so it can be knotted.
tools.description: Builds the rope as a MuJoCo elastic cable from its length, radius, segment count, bending and twisting stiffness, mass per metre and colour, with end caps (ferrules) and a mocap grip per end that can be welded to a hand. Given `centreline` (the measured polyline: measure_rope's centreline_rig / points, its whole result dict or that JSON file, in the scene's rig/world frame) the cable is BUILT along it: resampled by arc length to `segments` vertices (default one per 15 mm, 20 to 160), so its compiled pose lies where the video has it and length, pos and yaw follow from the points; 2-D points get z = radius (lying on the table). `rest_vertices` does the same with the vertices given exactly. A length, pos or yaw_deg that contradicts the points, or both centreline and rest_vertices, is refused rather than silently ignored. Without either the rope is straight along +x from pos. Helpers reset the centreline to a measured polyline, grab and release an end, and read the centreline back. Self-collision is on, which is the property without which a knot is not a knot. The cable_drag_test verifier drags a built rope and checks stretch, span and self-contact.

tools.name: construct_sponge_pad
tools.title: Construct sponge pad
tools.summary: A soft rectangular foam pad as a free body: a backing slab plus an nx x ny grid of foam cells, each on a sprung slide joint normal to the pad, so a pressing palm squashes it locally with a measured overall stiffness while it slides on the table with friction.
tools.description: Compliance is modelled as a bed of springs: the pad's bottom `base_frac` of the thickness is a rigid slab (the free root body, which touches the table) and the rest is split into nx x ny box cells, each a child body on a slide joint along the pad normal with range [-max_compression_frac x cell height, 0], stiffness stiffness_N_per_m / (nx ny) (cells act in parallel, so a uniform press of F newtons squashes the pad by F / stiffness_N_per_m), critical damping and a small armature for numerical stability. An uneven press (fingers on one end) squashes only the cells under it, which is how the pad 'bends' under the fingers; the slab itself stays flat. The mass is density x volume (or `mass`), shared by volume. Origin at the centre of the bottom face, length along x, width along y. Sites: top (centre of the top face) and grip (centre of the slab). Unknown parameters raise ValueError.

tools.title: Construct an interlocking stud brick
tools.summary: A toy building brick (LEGO, DUPLO, MEGA BLOKS style) as one free rigid body with an N x M stud grid on top and a hollow underside sized to seat over the studs of a brick below, so bricks stack and interlock.
tools.description: Builds an MJCF with one free body: a top plate, four skirt walls from the table up to the plate, underside tubes at the centres between every 2x2 group of studs (posts between the studs of a one-stud-wide brick), and studs_x x studs_y studs at the given pitch. The outer size is studs * pitch - edge_gap. The skirt wall thickness and tube radius are DERIVED from the stud radius and the requested clearance, so the studs of a brick below fit inside the skirt with `clearance` metres of play at the walls and the tubes. Each stud is a visual cylinder (no contact) plus a collision cylinder with straight sides (the lateral interlock) topped by an ellipsoid cap covering lead_in_frac of the stud height: the round cap is a lead-in that centres a brick released up to about clearance + stud_radius off. The body frame is at the centre of the bottom face (z = 0 on the table), x along studs_x. Mass comes from `mass` when given (density is rescaled), otherwise from `density` on the geom volumes. The stud caps take contact priority with a low cap_friction so the lead-in works; clutch_margin gives the straight stud sides a contact margin larger than the clearance, so a seated brick is held by a soft press-fit preload (friction clutch) instead of geometry alone; 0 turns it off. Assumes a rigid plastic brick.

tools.name: construct_tape_dispenser
tools.title: Construct a desk tape dispenser
tools.summary: A desk tape dispenser as a static (or free) rigid body: weighted base, tape roll between two cheeks and a sloped cutter arm overhanging the front with a clamp gap under its tip, plus a declared clamp site where a cord end held under the front can be anchored.
tools.description: Builds one MJCF body whose origin is the bottom centre of the footprint, +x pointing to the cutter (front), z up. The base is a box over the rear (1 - nose_frac) of the length and base_height high. Two cheek plates rise from the base at the rear to the full height and hold a tape roll (a cylinder along y, radius roll_radius, width roll_width; its cardboard core is a visual-only disk). A sloped cutter arm runs from the cheeks' front down to the front end of the footprint, where its underside stays clamp_gap above the table: the space under the overhang is free of geometry, so a cord, ribbon or tape end can lie there. The site '<name>_clamp' marks that spot on the table under the arm (the point a cord end held under the front is anchored to). Every touchable part (base, cheeks, roll, arm) is a colliding box or cylinder whose surface is the visual one; the mass is spread over them by volume. fixed=True builds a jointless body (scenery: the dispenser stays where it is staged); fixed=False adds a free joint. Unknown parameters and a roll that does not fit between the base and the top (or a nose so long that the cheeks overhang the base) are refused with a message naming the parameter.

tools.name: construct_tip_box
tools.title: Construct pipette tip box
tools.summary: A hinged-lid tip box: navy base, a tray of 96 tip collars and a translucent lid on a hinge, with the tips standing in it.
tools.description: Builds the base, the tray of tip collars on a grid, the hinged lid and the tips in their wells, from box dimensions, grid and pitch, lid hinge stiffness and colours; tipbox_well_xy() gives a well position by row and column. The moulded tips of the other wells are drawn as collar stubs and collide as slightly thinner cylinders of the same height (clear of a free tip in the next well), so nothing drawn stands outside the physics; the lid takes lid_mass spread over its plates and MuJoCo derives its inertia from them. tools.name: construct_tip_box_lowpoly
tools.title: Construct pipette tip box (low-poly collision, named tips)
tools.summary: A hinged-lid pipette tip box (free tips named by the caller) whose tray of tips collides as a few merged slabs with caged sockets for the real (free) tips, a lid with inertia from its own plates, and free tips with a lighter snap ring: the construct_tip_box mechanism at a contact budget a hand scene can afford.
tools.description: A fork of construct_tip_box, with caller-named free tips (tip_names), for scenes a robot hand works in. The original builds one collision box per tray cell (96+), draws the standing tips as visual-only stubs that stick 15 mm out of the physics, gives the lid a hand-written 1e-7 kg m^2 inertia and puts 37 collision geoms on every free tip, so a hand near the box is paired with 150 geoms and could sink into the drawn tips without contact. Here: the base is four walls and a floor (a hollow box, as box_enclosure_check expects); the tray is the region of the grid minus the free wells, cut into the fewest axis-aligned slabs (bands of rows split around each free well's square hole) that rise from the tray's underside to `slab_rise` above the tray top (default: 4 mm under the tips' collar tops, so the drawn collars stick out less than a 5 mm visual tolerance); the tray margins are part of those slabs; every free well keeps the platform column its tip's foot stands on and the slab hole (the collar's polygon plus `hole_clear`) cages the collar; the drawn collars of the other wells are visual cylinders on the slab top. The lid is the same friction hinge (with a stiff friction impedance, so it holds its own weight) and the same plates; MuJoCo infers its mass and inertia from them at `lid_density` (lid_end_walls_collide False makes the two short skirt walls visual only, inside the hull of the rest). Free tips are the micropipette family's tip (same collar, rim, lip radius and snap depth) with `lip_segments` lip capsules (>= 12 keeps the worst-yaw interference with the nose jaws positive; 8 does not) and the two fine shaft sections merged into one cylinder. Returns the same build dictionary as construct_tip_box plus the collision geom counts.

tools.name: construct_whiteboard
tools.title: Construct whiteboard
tools.summary: A framed whiteboard whose writing face is a live texture, so drawing and erasing change the object's own state.
tools.description: Builds an aluminium-framed board with a panel geom whose +Z face is the writing area, from the board size, frame width, thickness, colours and placement. The panel box is collision-only (group 3, no material) and a visual-only UV-mapped mesh <name>_face on it shows the texture, so Stage 4 and appearance_texture_check keep it (a texture on a box is dropped). The face carries a live texture (InkSurface in common/ink.py): a marker nib pressed onto the face stamps ink into it and an eraser face wipes it, and the texture is uploaded back into the renderer each frame, so "did the robot write a 4" and "is it gone" are questions about the board's state. Returns the panel geom, its texture handle and the texels-per-metre so a tool can map a world point to a texel. The ink_round_trip_test verifier proves a built board.

tools.name: diagnose_stage3_failure
tools.title: Diagnose a Stage 3 failure
tools.summary: Reads a failed finish verdict (or failure_report.json / gate_suite_report.json), the executor's outcomes and the workspace's poses, classifies the failure (unreachable, no stress-test pass, slip in carry, hand-hand or arm collision, joint speed, goal not met, Stage 4 cannot randomize, physics audit, upstream suspect, thin object, needs a steadying hand) with the evidence for each, and returns ranked concrete repairs: library tool names with arguments filled from the workspace, report_blocked with upstream for an earlier stage's error.
tools.description: The Stage 3 harness appends this diagnosis to every failed finish verdict, so the agent always gets next steps; the agent may also call it on an executor failure. Sources, all optional: the verdict ({ok, issues, reports}: the manifest check and stage3_gate_suite findings, or a failure_report.json with last_verdict / last_finish and the blocked reason, or a gate_suite_report.json), the newest executor outcomes.json files in the workspace (each failed entry's failed checks and measurements), the manifest, and the pose files. Text findings are matched against each class's vocabulary (gate names and the executor's check names, e.g. arm_unreachable, plan_collision, arm_speed, no_slip, stage4_physics_replay_gate). Executor checks are classed by the motion they failed in: rise / in_hand / pads_touching / servo_tracking in a grasp are a grasp that does not hold (no stress-test pass), in_hand or no_slip in a carry is slip, a joint that did not travel while the object's base moved, or a disturbed body of the same object, needs a steadying hand. Two classes are MEASURED from the scene, not read: thin_object (the top of the part the failing grasp is on, or of each manipulated object when nothing executed, is lower above the table than two fingertip pad radii of the setup hand plus 2 mm, so the pads cannot get under it) and upstream_suspect (a hand scene in poses/ whose object bodies differ from the bench scene's same bodies in collision geoms or extent: the Stage 2 asset the grasp tools see is not the object the robot meets; human prior warnings that the demonstration and the reconstruction disagree; a consistency check that says an earlier stage must be revised). Each class gets a score (measured evidence weighs most, the latest outcomes next, gate findings and the blocked reason after) and its repairs: optimize_grasp_pose with the failing pose as the start, human_grasp_seeds, optimize_pose_for_reach, whole-motion reach screening, a slower leg and execute_subgoal_plan(resume=True, from_subgoal=k), a park of the idle arm, a steadying hold first, generate_flat_pinches or a non-prehensile push for a thin part, report_blocked(upstream=...) with independently measured evidence. Finite failed grasp/contact searches do not establish unreachable upstream geometry. Preserve the configured stations and task goals. It changes nothing; it reads and advises.

tools.summary: Video inpainting of the erase masks (hands, arms, objects) with the VOID object-removal model, then a static clean plate: real pixels wherever the background is ever uncovered, VOID only where it never is.
tools.description: Photoreal robot data is the rendered robot composited onto the real background, so the human and whatever the simulation re-creates must leave the footage. Masks are dilated and scaled about their centroids so the faint outline an inpainter leaves falls inside them; VOID gets a quad-mask (remove / interaction ring where shadows live / keep) and a background prompt and runs over windows of 85 frames. Its pixels are adopted inside the mask always and in the ring only where it changed them. For a static camera one plate is then assembled as the per-pixel median over uncovered frames, with frames whose white balance was still settling dropped. Needs the VOID checkout and the CogVideoX-Fun 5B weights (several minutes on a GPU).

tools.name: estimate_gravity
tools.title: Estimate gravity
tools.summary: GeoCalib per-frame gravity, aggregated by a confidence-weighted spherical mean with MAD outlier rejection.
tools.description: A reconstruction needs to know which camera direction is down before it can place a table plane or stand an object upright. GeoCalib estimates the gravity vector in the camera frame from a single image; this runs it on a subsample of frames, discards frames whose estimate sits more than a few median absolute deviations from the median, and averages the rest weighted by GeoCalib's own confidence. The result is one unit vector in camera coordinates with its roll and pitch in degrees. Assumes the camera does not move during the clip.

inputs.description: Outlier cut in MADs. Default 3.

tools.name: execute_isaac_deformables
tools.title: Execute deformables in Isaac Sim
tools.summary: Runs the cords (ropes, cables, strings) of an executed Stage 3 episode in Isaac Sim / PhysX, driven by the robot motion MuJoCo executed: hands hold cords with compliant welds, rigid objects are kinematic colliders; writes the Isaac recording, its MuJoCo mirror (scene + trajectory) for the gates, and the episode video.
tools.description: DexAgent simulates deformable objects in Isaac Sim and everything else in MuJoCo. After execute_subgoal_plan has executed the robot (and the rigid objects) in MuJoCo, this tool replays that executed trajectory in Isaac Sim with every deformable of the Stage 2 scene simulated as the cord Stage 2 verified (scene_recon.json objects with simulator 'isaac' and their isaac.cord_json: geometry, PhysX coefficients and the settled link poses). Per video frame the MuJoCo row is put through forward kinematics: the robot and objects are posed, rigid objects are kinematic colliders, each hand drives a kinematic anchor, all interpolated over the physics substeps. GRASPS: `grasps` [{side, cord, weld_frame, release_frame, link (optional), stiff, slip_m, capture_m}], else read from the trajectory's labels: a run of frames in which a hand's label names the cord with a holding verb (grip, lift, carry, hold, lay, drag, pull, tuck, thread, cross, fold, place, move) is one grasp. At weld_frame the anchor is welded to the link nearest the hand's thumb-index pinch point (or `link` when it is within reach) if it is within capture_m (default 3 cm); else nothing is held and the grasp is reported missed. A weld lets go at release_frame, or earlier when the link is pulled further than slip_m from where the hand holds it, fading out over the cord's fade_frames. `events` [{frame, cord, bend_stiffness}] retune a cord during the episode. Outputs: isaac/isaac_recording.npz (every link's pose per frame, welds, strains, peak link speeds), isaac/isaac_events.json, deformables.json (the cords, grasps and events: what a replay needs), isaac_episode_report.json (grasps held / missed / slipped, peak and over-limit link speeds, the lowest link against the table, PhysX errors and invalid transforms, and the sha256 binding of scene, trajectory, cord specifications and scripts that isaac_recording_check re-checks); scene_mirror.xml (the executed scene plus each cord as a construct_rope-named MuJoCo cable that MuJoCo never steps) and trajectory_mirror.npz (the executed qpos plus the cords' recorded link poses, labels and segments), on which the gates that read object states run unchanged; sim_video.mp4 when render is on (the registered camera, Isaac RTX). Fails (ok false, issues) on PhysX errors, a non-finite pose, a missed grasp, a link below the table by more than 3 mm or a peak link speed above max_link_speed.

tools.name: execute_subgoal_plan
tools.title: Execute subgoal plan
tools.summary: Run a list of subgoals end to end: plan each one's keyframes from the executed state of the previous one, roll it out in contact physics, check its expectations, and stop at the first subgoal that fails; writes the actual rigid robot episode with phases, recorded controls and per-subgoal outcomes.
tools.description: The Stage 3 driver. The hand is bolted to its arm, so the arm is planned with the hand (couple_arms) and a subgoal the arm cannot hold is re-solved (next grasp candidate, pose turned for reach, carried object turned) before any physics. The arm fill is collision aware (common/armplan.py): a free-space leg whose straight joint path runs the arm, its hand or what it carries into the table, an object, the other station or its own hand is replaced by an RRT-Connect path (shortcut, corners smoothed, 20/10/5 mm clearance) with the same ends, an idle station (its hand still and touching nothing) that comes within 3 cm of the active one is parked at a clearance configuration and comes back on its own next reach, and legs too fast for the arm (90 deg/s, 12 rad/s^2 smoothed, 4.8 m/s^2 at the flange) are slowed with contact phases kept at their pace; if an otherwise passing physical trial exceeds the arm speed cap, the same joint path is retried more slowly at most twice from the identical complete initial state. Every gate is rerun, integration-step velocities determine the speed peak, and failed timing trials remain in the segment's timing_attempts folder. a clean straight plan is left exactly as it was, and the subgoal's measured.arm.plan lists what was planned, parked or could not be. A one-hand entry whose planned hand runs more than 3 mm into the other (still) hand fails as hand_clearance before physics. For subgoal k it calls plan_subgoal_keyframes from the physics state at the end of subgoal k-1 (hand commands carried over so a holding hand keeps pressing), rollout_keyframes_physics on the keyframes, and the outcome evaluation on the executed frames (rise, in hand, no slip, at target, released, at rest, supported, joint reached, turned, tilted, untouched objects, penetration, servo tracking). A required stable-grasp check cannot be disabled with expect.no_slip=False, redirected to a different object/hand, or shortened with slip_from; the executed phases determine its window. The slip tolerance can only be tightened. A failing subgoal stops the run with its measurements so the pose or the parameters can be changed and the run resumed from that subgoal (`resume=True` keeps the finished segments on disk; every plan entry has its own segment folder, subgoal_NN, or subgoal_NN_SS for entries that share an index: their `step`, else the next free step number in plan order, so entries never overwrite each other). A two-hand entry ({motion: 'both', hands: {left: entry, right: entry}, sync}) runs both hands' plans in ONE rollout, time-aligned: both arms are planned with their hands (each with its own free-space legs, each planned against the other arm and hand where they are at the same time: a leg that would meet them first waits along its own straight path, else takes a planned path, retimed together), the planned hands must stay hand_clearance_m apart (else the attempt fails as hand_clearance before physics), and each hand's expectations are checked with the bystanders and hands_apart; lift_together and carry_together (two hands on one cable) run the same way. An isolated grasp stress pass is a candidate screen: mounted-arm contact dynamics and another hand acting on the same object can still change the grasp. A rise/contact/slip failure requires a changed grasp, approach or timing followed by a fresh physical trial from the same valid prefix. For lift_together, approach_controls reports the waypoint offsets and synchronized contact timings used in the reference; an agent can verify that its proposed repair changed the plan. A pin (one hand steadying a part while the other acts) lasts through the following entries: the pinning hand keeps its commands and, for a press, its wrist force cap, and every such entry is judged on the pinned part staying put on every frame (`pinned`). A press_seat entry runs with the wrist force cap its plan asks for (at most the 40 N default). A grip clamps the grip fingers press_depth_rad past their closed targets (torque-capped); a negative press_depth_rad (on the pose or the entry) drives them that far toward extension instead, spreading what they hold (scissor rings). The episode is written as trajectory.npz paired with scene_physics.xml: the actual rigid robot's named joint states and controls, including every integration step. Proposal diagnostics use separate files. Failed executions have no formal trajectory. execution_report.json binds the scene, trajectory, and each selected/re-anchored pose to its starting hand scene.

With cut rules every physics step checks scissors.try_sever on each join, trajectory.npz / trajectory_hands.npz carry eq_active [T, neq] (the equality state after each frame), eq_active_start and eq_names, and the summary lists `cuts` [{equality, frame, subgoal}]; with latch rules the summary lists `latches` [{equality, event: engage | release, frame, subgoal}] read from that record and each subgoal's outcome its `latches` events; scenes without such rules are run and written exactly as before.
